questions.group: Set A — Subject–Verb Attraction (the "of" phrase steals your verb)
questions.question:
Choose the correct verb.
The *list* of eligible candidates ___ been published on the notice board.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** The subject is *the list* (singular). The verb agrees with the head noun, not with *candidates* inside the "of" phrase: *the list ... has been published.*
**Common wrong answer: (a) have.** People let the nearest plural noun *candidates* pull the verb into the plural.
questions.trick: Mentally delete the "of ___" phrase. "The list ___ been published" — obviously *has*.

questions.group: Set A — Subject–Verb Attraction (the "of" phrase steals your verb)
questions.question:
Choose the correct verb.
The *quality* of the answers submitted by the trainees ___ improved sharply this quarter.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** Head noun *quality* is singular → *has improved*. *Answers* and *trainees* are just modifiers.
**Common wrong answer: (a) have.** The plural *answers* sitting right before the blank tempts the plural verb.
questions.trick: Find the true subject by asking "what improved?" — the *quality*, not the answers.

questions.group: Set A — Subject–Verb Attraction (the "of" phrase steals your verb)
questions.question:
Choose the correct verb.
A *bunch* of keys ___ lying on the manager's desk since morning.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *A bunch* is a singular collective head → *a bunch ... has been lying*. The tense needs perfect-continuous with "since morning," so "has been."
**Common wrong answer: (a) are / (c) have been.** *Keys* right before the verb screams plural.
questions.trick: "Since morning" demands a perfect form, and the singular subject fixes it to *has been*.

questions.group: Set A — Subject–Verb Attraction (the "of" phrase steals your verb)
questions.question:
Choose the correct verb.
The *series* of workshops on financial literacy ___ scheduled for the last week of August.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Series* is singular even though it ends in -s and refers to many workshops → *the series ... is scheduled*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) are.** The -s ending and the many workshops both suggest plural.
questions.trick: *Series, species, means, news* look plural but take a singular verb.

questions.group: Set A — Subject–Verb Attraction (the "of" phrase steals your verb)
questions.question:
Choose the correct verb.
Neither the *branch manager* nor his *assistants* ___ aware of the revised circular.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** With *neither ... nor*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. The nearer one is *assistants* (plural) → *were*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) was.** People default to singular after "neither."
questions.trick: In neither/nor and either/or, the verb obeys whichever subject is closest to it.

questions.group: Set B — "The number of" vs "A number of"
questions.question:
Choose the correct verb.
The *number* of applicants for the clerical post ___ risen every year since 2019.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *The number of ___* is singular (it names one figure) → *the number ... has risen*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) have.** *Applicants* just before the verb drags it plural.
questions.trick: "The number" = one number = singular. Always.

questions.group: Set B — "The number of" vs "A number of"
questions.question:
Choose the correct verb.
A *number* of employees ___ requested a transfer to the regional office.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *A number of ___* means "several/many" and is plural → *a number of employees have requested*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) has.** People overcorrect after learning that "the number" is singular and apply it to "a number" too.
questions.trick: THE number → singular; A number → plural. Swap "a number of" with "many" to hear the plural.

questions.group: Set B — "The number of" vs "A number of"
questions.question:
Choose the correct verb.
The *number* of defaulters ___ surprisingly small this financial year.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *The number of* → singular → *the number ... is small*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) are.** *Defaulters* pulls it plural.
questions.trick: Same as Q6 — "the number" is one quantity, so *is*.

questions.group: Set C — Since vs For (a point in time vs a stretch of time)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
She has been working at this bank ___ 2015.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Since* marks a *point* in time (a start date). 2015 is a point → *since 2015*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) for.** Learners pair "for" with any duration, forgetting that a fixed year is a point.
questions.trick: SINCE + a point on the calendar/clock; FOR + a length of time.

questions.group: Set C — Since vs For (a point in time vs a stretch of time)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
They have known each other ___ nearly a decade.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Nearly a decade* is a *duration* → *for nearly a decade*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) since.** The present-perfect "have known" makes people reach for "since" reflexively.
questions.trick: If you can put "a period of" in front of it (a period of nearly a decade), use FOR.

questions.group: Set C — Since vs For (a point in time vs a stretch of time)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
The audit team has been examining the ledgers ___ last Monday.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Last Monday* is a specific starting point → *since last Monday*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) for.** "Last Monday" feels like recent time, so "for" slips in.
questions.trick: "Last Monday" answers "starting when?" — a point — so SINCE.

questions.group: Set D — Senior / Superior / Prefer + TO (never "than")
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
He is three years ___ me in service, so he chairs the committee.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** Latin-origin comparatives (*senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, anterior*) take *to*, never *than* — and never "more." → *senior to me*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) senior than / (b) more senior than.** English comparison habit ("taller than") makes "than" feel natural.
questions.trick: Words ending in -ior lean on *to*, not *than*.

questions.group: Set D — Senior / Superior / Prefer + TO (never "than")
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
Most reviewers agree that this model is far ___ the earlier one in battery life.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Superior* is already comparative and takes *to* → *superior to the earlier one*. "More superior" is a double comparative.
**Common wrong answer: (a) superior than / (c) more superior to.** Both the "than" reflex and the urge to add "more" strike here.
questions.trick: Never say "more superior." Superior *to*. Done.

questions.group: Set D — Senior / Superior / Prefer + TO (never "than")
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
I would ___ tea to coffee on a cold morning.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Prefer X to Y*. Here the structure is "prefer tea to coffee," so the verb is simply *prefer*. (Options a and d are identical in wording; the intended correct verb is *prefer*, completing *prefer tea to coffee*.)
**Common wrong answer: (b) rather / (e) prefer than.** People confuse it with "would rather ... than," which is a different pattern.
questions.trick: PREFER pairs with *to*. Only "would rather" pairs with *than*.

questions.group: Set D — Senior / Superior / Prefer + TO (never "than")
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
Given the choice, most customers ___ digital statements ___ paper ones.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Prefer A to B* → *prefer digital statements to paper ones*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) prefer / than.** The comparison "feels" like it needs "than."
questions.trick: Chant it: "prefer TEA to COFFEE" — the slot after prefer's object is always *to*.

questions.group: Set E — Less vs Fewer (uncountable vs countable)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
There were ___ candidates in this shift than in the morning one.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Candidates* are countable → *fewer*. (*Less* is for uncountables.)
**Common wrong answer: (a) less.** "Less" is the default filler for everyone in speech.
questions.trick: If you can put a number in front (ten candidates), use FEWER.

questions.group: Set E — Less vs Fewer (uncountable vs countable)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
We spent ___ money on marketing this year, yet reached more people.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Money* as a mass/uncountable idea → *less money*. (You'd count *rupees*, not *money*.)
**Common wrong answer: (a) fewer.** After drilling "fewer," students overcorrect onto uncountables.
questions.trick: Money, water, time, information → uncountable → LESS.

questions.group: Set E — Less vs Fewer (uncountable vs countable)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
The express counter is for shoppers with ___ than ten items.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Items* are countable → *fewer than ten items*. (This is exactly why "10 items or fewer" is the correct sign.)
**Common wrong answer: (a) less.** Supermarket "10 items or less" signs have trained the wrong reflex.
questions.trick: Countable plural noun after the blank → FEWER.

questions.group: Set F — Correlatives (no sooner…than, hardly…when, not only…but also, either…or)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
No sooner ___ the results announced ___ the students began celebrating.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *No sooner* is followed by *than* (not "when"/"then"). With inversion after a fronted negative you invert subject and auxiliary: *No sooner were the results announced than...*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) had / when or (d) did / than.** People pair "no sooner" with "when," or force "had" where a passive "were" is needed.
questions.trick: NO SOONER ... THAN (they rhyme in the pairing); HARDLY/SCARCELY ... WHEN.

questions.group: Set F — Correlatives (no sooner…than, hardly…when, not only…but also, either…or)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
Hardly had the train left the platform ___ the signal failed.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Hardly/Scarcely ... when* is the fixed pair → *Hardly had the train left ... when the signal failed*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) than.** "No sooner ... than" bleeds over onto "hardly."
questions.trick: Hardly and Scarcely shake hands with WHEN. Only "no sooner" takes THAN.

questions.group: Set F — Correlatives (no sooner…than, hardly…when, not only…but also, either…or)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
She is ___ a talented singer ___ a gifted teacher.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** The matching correlative is *not only ... but also*.
**Common wrong answer: (b) not only / but.** Dropping "also" breaks the balanced pair in a formal test context.
questions.trick: Keep correlatives in their fixed sets — "not only" always wants "but also."

questions.group: Set F — Correlatives (no sooner…than, hardly…when, not only…but also, either…or)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
___ the manager ___ the cashier was present when the vault was opened.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Neither* pairs only with *nor* → *Neither the manager nor the cashier was present*.
**Common wrong answer: (b) Neither / or.** "Or" feels interchangeable with "nor."
questions.trick: Neither↔Nor, Either↔Or. Same first letter after the slash: **n**either/**n**or.

questions.group: Set G — Redundancy (say it once)
questions.question:
Pick the option that best replaces the underlined part.
Please *return back* the signed form by Friday.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Return* already means "give/send back," so "return back" is redundant → just *return*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) return back / (b) revert back.** Both are everyday spoken redundancies ("revert back" doubles the "back" inside re-).
questions.trick: Any verb with "re-" (return, revert, repeat, reply) rejects a following "back/again."

questions.group: Set G — Redundancy (say it once)
questions.question: Pick the sentence that is free of redundancy.
options: The two firms decided to mutually cooperate with each other.
The two firms decided to cooperate.
The two firms decided to mutually cooperate.
The two firms decided to cooperate with each other mutually.
The two firms decided to co-jointly cooperate.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Cooperate* already contains "with each other/mutually," so those additions are redundant. The clean sentence is (b).
**Common wrong answer: (a) or (c).** "Mutually cooperate" and "cooperate with each other" sound emphatic, so they seem richer.
questions.trick: "Co-" and "mutual/each other" are the same idea — keep one.

questions.group: Set G — Redundancy (say it once)
questions.question:
Pick the option that best replaces the underlined part.
The committee will *repeat that point again* in the next meeting.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Repeat* means "say again," so "again" is redundant → *repeat that point*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) repeat that point again.** It's a near-universal spoken habit.
questions.trick: Repeat = again already inside it. Don't stack another "again."

questions.group: Set G — Redundancy (say it once)
questions.question: Pick the sentence with no redundancy.
options: The final outcome of the merger is still uncertain.
The end result of the merger is still uncertain.
The outcome of the merger is still uncertain.
The final end result of the merger is still uncertain.
The outcome result of the merger is still uncertain.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Outcome* and *result* are the same idea; "final outcome," "end result," and "final end result" all double up. Clean version: (c).
**Common wrong answer: (a) final outcome / (b) end result.** They sound like standard business English.
questions.trick: An outcome/result is inherently the end thing — drop "final/end."

questions.group: Set H — Past Perfect & Sequence of Tenses (the earlier action takes "had")
questions.question:
Choose the correct form.
By the time the ambulance arrived, the patient ___ already ___.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** Of two past events, the *earlier* one takes past perfect. Recovery happened before the arrival → *had already recovered*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) has ... recovered.** Mixing present perfect into a wholly past narration.
questions.trick: "By the time X happened, Y had already happened." The action further back gets HAD.

questions.group: Set H — Past Perfect & Sequence of Tenses (the earlier action takes "had")
questions.question:
Choose the correct form.
The train ___ before we ___ the station.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** With *before/after*, the conjunction already fixes the sequence, so a simple past in both clauses is standard and correct: *The train left before we reached the station.* (Using "had left" is also acceptable, but among the options, the clean simple-past pair is the intended answer; "reached had" combinations in the other options are wrong.)
**Common wrong answer: (d) left / had reached.** Putting "had" on the *later* action (reaching) reverses the real order.
questions.trick: "Before" already shows what came first, so don't force "had" onto the second, later action.

questions.group: Set H — Past Perfect & Sequence of Tenses (the earlier action takes "had")
questions.question:
Choose the correct form.
She told the auditor that she ___ the discrepancy the previous week.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** Reported speech in the past: the earlier noticing shifts to past perfect → *she had noticed ... the previous week*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) has noticed.** Failing to back-shift the tense after "told."
questions.trick: After a past reporting verb (told/said), an earlier action becomes HAD + past participle.

questions.group: Set H — Past Perfect & Sequence of Tenses (the earlier action takes "had")
questions.question:
Choose the correct form.
When I reached the counter, the officer ___ for lunch.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** Leaving happened before reaching the counter → past perfect *had already left*.
**Common wrong answer: (e) already left / (a) has already left.** Simple past blurs the order; present perfect clashes with the past frame.
questions.trick: Two past actions, one clearly first → first one wears HAD.

questions.group: Set I — Article a / an by SOUND (not by spelling)
questions.question:
Choose the correct article.
He completed the internship in ___ hour and a half.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** Choose a/an by the *sound* of the next word. *Hour* starts with a silent H, a vowel sound /aʊ/ → *an hour*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) a.** The written consonant "h" fools the eye.
questions.trick: Say the word aloud. If it opens with a vowel *sound*, use "an" — spelling is irrelevant.

questions.group: Set I — Article a / an by SOUND (not by spelling)
questions.question:
Choose the correct article.
She is pursuing ___ MBA after five years in the field.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *MBA* begins with the letter M, pronounced "em" — a vowel sound /e/ → *an MBA*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) a.** "M is a consonant" thinking ignores how the abbreviation is voiced.
questions.trick: For abbreviations, use the letter's spoken name: M = "em," so "an."

questions.group: Set I — Article a / an by SOUND (not by spelling)
questions.question:
Choose the correct article.
The professor is ___ European scholar of monetary history.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *European* starts with a "y" consonant sound /juː/ → *a European*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) an.** The written vowel "E" invites "an."
questions.trick: "Eu-" and "Uni-" words sound like "you-" — a consonant sound — so use "a" (a European, a university, a useful tool).

questions.group: Set I — Article a / an by SOUND (not by spelling)
questions.question:
Choose the correct article.
It was ___ honest mistake, and the clerk apologised at once.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Honest* has a silent H → vowel sound /ɒ/ → *an honest mistake*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) a.** The consonant letter "h" again.
questions.trick: The silent-H club — honest, hour, honour, heir — all take "an."

questions.group: Set I — Article a / an by SOUND (not by spelling)
questions.question:
Choose the correct article.
The scheme requires every applicant to hold ___ university degree.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *University* opens with a "yoo" consonant sound → *a university degree*.
**Common wrong answer: (a) an.** The letter "u" looks like a vowel.
questions.trick: If the word sounds like it starts with "y," it takes "a." (a university, a European, a one-time offer).

questions.group: Set J — Para-jumble Openers & the Pronoun-Hug (a pronoun must follow its noun)
questions.question:
Which sentence is the correct *opening* sentence of the paragraph?
(P) It quickly became the most downloaded app in the country.
(Q) In 2021, a small startup launched a budgeting tool aimed at first-time earners.
(R) They had built it in just four months.
(S) Its clean design won over sceptical users.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** The opener must introduce the subject with a *full noun*, not a pronoun. Only (Q) — "a small startup launched a budgeting tool" — names things fresh. P's *It*, R's *They/it*, and S's *Its* all point back to nouns in Q, so they can't come first.
**Common wrong answer: (a) P.** "It quickly became the most downloaded app" reads like a punchy headline opener, but "It" has no antecedent yet.
questions.trick: A sentence starting with a pronoun (It/They/This/Its) can never open a paragraph — it needs an earlier noun to hug.

questions.group: Set J — Para-jumble Openers & the Pronoun-Hug (a pronoun must follow its noun)
questions.question:
Which pair must stay together, in this order?
(1) The RBI released the new guidelines on Monday.
(2) They took effect the very next day.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *They* in (2) refers to *the new guidelines* in (1), so (1) must come first and (2) must follow immediately — the pronoun hugs its noun.
**Common wrong answer: (a) 2 then 1.** Testing whether you'll place the pronoun before its antecedent.
questions.trick: Noun first, pronoun right behind it — never the reverse.

questions.group: Set J — Para-jumble Openers & the Pronoun-Hug (a pronoun must follow its noun)
questions.question: Which sentence *cannot* be the opener?
options: A new library opened near the market last week.
The mayor inaugurated a modern facility on Ring Road.
This has delighted the students of the area.
Volunteers had spent months cataloguing the books.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *This* is a demonstrative pronoun with no antecedent yet, so (c) cannot open. (Also, (d) "had spent" is a past-perfect follow-up that needs an earlier past event to relate to, but the clearest impossible opener is the pronoun-led (c).)
**Common wrong answer: (d) Volunteers had spent months...** Its past perfect feels mid-story, but it at least names a full subject; the demonstrative "This" in (c) is the definitive non-opener.
questions.trick: Opening lines can't lead with This/That/These/Those/It/They — they all need a prior noun.

questions.group: Set K — Contrast Connectors (Despite/In spite of + noun; Although/Though + clause)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
___ the heavy rain, the outdoor recruitment drive went ahead as planned.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** *Despite / In spite of* are followed by a *noun/noun phrase*. "The heavy rain" is a noun phrase → *Despite the heavy rain*. (Although/Though/While would need a full clause with a verb.)
**Common wrong answer: (a) Although.** People treat all contrast words as interchangeable.
questions.trick: DESPITE + noun (no verb); ALTHOUGH + subject + verb. There's no verb after the blank here, so it must be *Despite*.

questions.group: Set K — Contrast Connectors (Despite/In spite of + noun; Although/Though + clause)
questions.question:
Fill in the blank.
___ she had prepared thoroughly, she felt nervous before the interview.
questions.solution:
**Rule:** "___ she had prepared thoroughly" is a full clause (subject *she* + verb *had prepared*) → it needs *Although*. *Despite/In spite of/Regardless of* would require a noun, not a clause.
**Common wrong answer: (a) Despite / (b) In spite of.** Both express contrast, so they tempt you, but they can't sit before a clause without "the fact that."
questions.trick: See a subject + verb after the blank? Use ALTHOUGH/THOUGH. See only a noun? Use DESPITE/IN SPITE OF. (*Owing to* means "because of," the wrong meaning entirely.)
